newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian parliament passes MMT ban.
newsitem.headline: Canadian parliament passes MMT ban.

text.p: The House of Commons, the lower chamber of Canada's Parliament, late on Monday passed a bill that would effectively ban the controversial gasoline additive MMT.
The final vote on the bill, which bans the import and interprovincial trade of MMT, took place after the Liberal government on Friday used its power to force an end to debate and called for a vote.
Oppostion parties had been stalling the bill's passage by repeatedly introducing amendments.
MMT -- or methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl -- is a fuel octane enhancer and has been used in Canada as a replacement for lead in gasoline since 1977.
Richmond, Va.-based Ethyl Corp 's Canadian subsidiary, Ethyl Canada, is the only importer and manufacturer of MMT in the country.
Two months ago Ethyl threatened the Canadian government with a US$200 million lawsuit under the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) in an effort to stop the bill.
Ethyl Canada president David Wilson said he would take his company's case to Canada's Senate, which must give final approval to the bill before it becomes law.
"The battle is far from over," Wilson said in a statement.

The MMT ban is supported by an unlikely coalition of health groups, environmentalists and automakers. While MMT boosts octane and reduces emissions of carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxide, all three groups advocate using other octane enhancers.
Environmentalists back claims by international automakers that MMT interferes with car diagnostic systems, and charge that manganese is a potential neurotoxin that might hurt human brain development.
The Coalition for Banning MMT was quick to praise Ottawa for its swift passage of the so-called Bill C-29.
"We congratulate the government for achieving progress on passing Bill C-29," Mark Nantais, president of the Motor Vehicle Manufacturers' Association, a member of the coalition, said in a statement.
The bill now goes to parliament's upper house, the Senate, for ratification. The appointed Senate usually passes government bills, but occasionally stalls or rejects them.
